newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US durable orders may fall, but trend up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US durable orders may fall, but trend up.

text.p: Despite the widespread belief that U.S. manufacturing is generally stronger this year, forecasts for August durable goods orders vary widely because monthly data has been volatile, economists said Tuesday.

Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, said he "guesses" data to be released Thursday will show little change in August durable goods orders. But he added that sharp variations would not surprise him that much.
"Remember, one order for one aircraft can skew the number significantly," Johnson said.
The data is scheduled for release on Thursday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Johnson noted the trend for durable goods orders has been up for the year with "enormous volatility."

Forecasts for overall durable goods orders by economists polled by Reuters ranged from up 2.0 percent to down 1.0 percent. The average forecast had orders down 0.1 percent in August, or off 0.7 percent excluding the volatile defense category.

Lee Youngdahl, vice president and an economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc, said aircraft orders should be reflected in August's number and bolster the current trend. Orders outside transportation were more modest, he said, but not modest enough to raise concerns of weakness.

"The trend that's underway is one of strength when you look back in four of the past five months," he said. "The underlying trend is good. Demand remains pretty solid and inventories are at pretty low levels."

James Padinha, economist at MMS International Inc., said he expects durable goods data will be unchanged in August. However, he noted that Boeing Co recently reported large aircraft orders that could skew the data upward if it is included in the August report.
If the Boeing order is included in August data, Padinha said he expects durable goods orders could jump 0.5 percent.
"It's unlikely the whole thing will show up in August, but if it does it seems like the potential is for a surprise on the upside," Padinha said.
Padinha expects the data will settle back from big gains in July. The overall trend remains strong, however, and the August data will not upset calls for firm numbers down the road, he said.

"The overall story is on a year-over-year basis orders are still doing pretty well," he said. "If you put recent orders in a category marked 'favors Fed tightening' or 'does not favor Fed tightening,' you'd probably have to put it in 'favors'."

Defense spending, which tends to go back and forth from month to month, should rebound from a big drop in July, Youngdahl said. And outside the more volatile sectors, he said he sees no other areas that might show inherent weakness. He noted primary metals and industrial machinery have both perked up in recent months after a slow start for the year.
Looking ahead, Youngdahl said he sees four to six months of an uptrend for durable goods based on expectations of rising capacity utilization rates.

"There is still some slack on the industrial capacity side of things, but with demand remaining good, I think the idea is factories continue to try and add capacity where they can," Youngdahl said, adding, "I would think that would tend to undergird orders going forward."
Slackening consumer demand will not derail businesses from rebuilding inventories to "a reasonable level," he said.
